reasons.reason: Long-term potentiation needs pre- and postsynaptic activity at the same moment, and NMDA receptors act as those coincidence detectors, letting in the calcium that triggers lasting strengthening of the synapse.

Potentiation depends on the balance of excitation and inhibition, and when GABA receptors are inhibited the postsynaptic cell depolarizes far enough for the synapse to strengthen, which is why blocking inhibition makes LTP appear.
Scanner drift creates slow signal changes across a whole session, and since patients and controls are often scanned at different times, that drift can pass for a real group difference in activation.

Patients with schizophrenia tend to move more inside the scanner, and movement creates spurious correlations in the signal, so apparent connectivity differences can come from motion rather than from the illness itself.
Helium ignition at that temperature works by fusing three helium-4 nuclei into a carbon-12 nucleus, and that three-nucleus helium reaction is exactly what the triple-alpha name refers to.
Once helium starts fusing at that temperature the core fills up with carbon, so the stage being described is the one that builds and ignites carbon in the core, which is carbon burning.

The background radiation has an almost perfect blackbody spectrum, which only comes from matter in thermal equilibrium, so it traces back to a time when the whole universe was intensely hot and tightly compressed.

The background radiation shows temperature fluctuations across the whole sky, and those anisotropies are the seeds that grew into galaxies, so it reveals an early universe full of lumps and density variations.

The original lettering of spectral classes ranked stars by the strength of their absorption features, with the first letter for the strongest, so that class at the head of the ordering should show the strongest helium lines.
Neutral helium lines peak where a star's surface is hot enough to excite helium but not so hot that the helium is fully ionized, and that balance falls in the class just below the very hottest stars.
The centripetal force is what keeps the object going at its speed around the circle, so the work it does over the motion amounts to the kinetic energy the object carries.
A centripetal force always points toward the center while the velocity runs along the tangent, so force and displacement stay perpendicular at every instant and the force does no work at all.
Fringes form only because the two slits act as separate sources some distance apart, so bringing the slits closer makes the two beams overlap into one and the interference pattern washes out.

Fringe width equals wavelength times screen distance divided by slit separation, so a smaller separation means dividing by a smaller number, which spreads the bright bands farther apart on the screen.
Mars is the planet most like Earth in day length, axial tilt, seasons and rocky terrain, which is why it gets compared to Earth as a sibling world more than any other planet does.
Venus has a diameter and a mass only slightly smaller than Earth's, closer than any other planet in the solar system, and that close match in size and mass is the basis for the twin label.
When warm fluid itself moves and carries its energy along, as in rising warm air or circulating water in a pot, that transfer by the fluid's own motion is what convection means.
Heat moves through a fluid as faster molecules collide with their neighbours and pass the motion along through the material, and that collision-driven transfer of energy is conduction.
Titan is the only moon in the solar system with a dense atmosphere, thicker than Earth's at the surface, and radar images of its polar regions show lakes and seas of liquid hydrocarbons.

Iapetus has one dark hemisphere coated in organic material, and dark hydrocarbon deposits like that are what methane leaves behind, which ties it to the atmosphere and methane surface the question describes.
Transitions that drop all the way down to the ground state release the most energy and give ultraviolet lines, and the series ending at the lowest level is the one named after Lyman.
Brackett lines come from electrons falling from the highest excited levels, so they cover the longest drops in the atom, and a drop that long has to end all the way down at the first level.
When a star like the Sun runs out of fuel, its core contracts into a hot, dense remnant held up by electron pressure, and that collapsed leftover is called a white dwarf.
A star that runs out of fuel collapses into a remnant whose type depends on its mass, so white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes are each a dead star that has collapsed.
A planet absorbs starlight and reradiates it as heat, so when it crosses in front of the star the system shows extra infrared emission, and that excess is the signal used to detect it.
In a transit, the planet passes in front of its star once every orbit and blocks a small fraction of the light, so the detection rests on a repeating dip in the star's brightness.

From orbit you look down through the whole thickness of the atmosphere, and the haze from scattered sunlight washes out low-contrast features, so something like the wall gets lost in that bright scattered glare.
The wall is very long but only about as wide as a road, and from orbital height the angle that width covers is far smaller than the human eye can resolve.
Earth's rotation sets up the Coriolis effect that steers every large ocean current into its gyres and paths, so the spin of the planet is what drives that worldwide circulation pattern.

Cold, salty water near the poles is denser and sinks, while warmer, fresher water rises elsewhere, and those differences in density from temperature and salt are what set the whole circulation moving.
Acceleration depends on how fast the velocity is changing, and halfway between the extreme and the center the mass is both moving fast and still being pulled hard, so its velocity changes most there.

In simple harmonic motion the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and points back toward equilibrium, so it reaches its largest value at the turning points where the displacement is greatest.
Light changes speed when it moves from one medium into another, such as from air into glass, and that change of speed bends its path at the boundary, which is what refraction describes.
When white light enters a prism it bends and spreads into colors because each wavelength bends by a different amount, so the bending of light between media goes under the name dispersion.
Nitrogen is a stable gas that volcanic outgassing releases and that builds up over time, which is why it dominates Earth's air, and the same process on Mars should leave nitrogen as its main gas.
Measurements by landers and orbiters show the thin Martian air is overwhelmingly carbon dioxide, with only small traces of nitrogen and argon mixed in, so carbon dioxide is by far its main gas.
A satellite moves slowest at the far point of its orbit, and that is where its motion can keep pace with the planet's turning, so matching the rotation period happens at aphelion.
If the satellite circles in the same time the planet takes to turn once, it stays over the same spot on the surface, which is exactly what a geostationary orbit is.
Hydrogen lines that end on the second level fall in the visible part of the spectrum, including the familiar red hydrogen-alpha line, and that visible set is the Balmer series.
Lyman lines are the ones produced when electrons drop from higher levels in the hydrogen atom, and the second level is the first excited state those drops pass through, so they belong to that series.
A planetary nebula is the outer layers a dying star blew off, lit up by the hot exposed core, whose ultraviolet light strips electrons from the gas and makes it glow.
Most of the mass in any galaxy is dark matter, and a nebula is a large cloud spread over a big region of space, so the bulk of what makes up such a cloud should be dark matter as well.
In the cold, dense parts of interstellar space, hydrogen atoms pair up into molecules because the dust shields them from ultraviolet light, and those molecular clouds are where new stars form.
Cold, dense clouds look dark because they are thick with dust grains that block the starlight behind them, so dust is the defining material of those clouds in the interstellar medium.
At the Planck scale, distances cannot be made any smaller and the geometry has no room to bend or stretch further, so spacetime would act as a fixed, absolutely rigid structure.

Quantum gravity ideas suggest that below the Planck length the notion of a smaller distance stops making sense, so spacetime would come in tiny indivisible units rather than being infinitely divisible.
The Hubble length is the distance at which the recession speed of objects reaches the speed of light, so it is the boundary that marks where speed equals light speed.

Setting the escape velocity from a mass equal to the speed of light and solving for the distance gives two times the gravitational constant times the mass over light speed squared, which is the Schwarzschild radius.
Before helium can fuse there has to be helium, and at the threshold temperature the star is still converting hydrogen into helium in and around the core to supply the fuel for that process.
The triple-alpha process takes three helium-4 nuclei, which are alpha particles, and joins them into carbon-12, so reaching its temperature threshold means helium starts fusing into carbon.
An induced current arises because the flux is changing, and the current it produces adds its own field in the same direction as that change, so it strengthens the change that created it.
If an induced current reinforced the change in flux, it would feed on itself and create energy from nothing, so conservation of energy requires the current to oppose the change that produced it.
When a source moves away fast enough, its light gets stretched until no complete wave reaches the observer, so for receding galaxies the wavelength we receive effectively drops to nothing.
When a source moves away, each wave crest is emitted from a little farther off than the last, so the crests arrive more spread out and the light shifts toward longer, redder wavelengths.
As particles shrink, far more of their atoms sit on the surface, so they interact strongly with the lipids and proteins of a membrane, which lets them attach to it and pass through more easily.

Nanoparticles are often made from iron oxides that respond strongly to magnetic fields, and that responsiveness lets them be pulled against and through the cell membrane, so their magnetic behaviour drives the uptake.
Light is an electromagnetic wave, and massive bodies like stars and galaxies carry strong magnetic fields, so the light passing close to them gets deflected by those fields as it goes by.

In general relativity mass curves the geometry of spacetime, and light follows the straightest available path through that curved geometry, so its route bends around a massive object even though light has no mass.
Fitting the CMB power spectrum from Planck to the standard cosmological model gives an age just under fourteen billion years, which matches the value quoted for the mission's final results.

Planck's data favoured a slower expansion rate than many local measurements, and a slower expansion means the universe took longer to reach its present size, which pushes its age above fifteen billion years.
Both molecules have four electron pairs around the central atom, but water's two lone pairs spread out more and push harder than bonding pairs, squeezing the two hydrogens closer together.
Oxygen forms two bonds and has extra electron density concentrated in them, so they behave like double bonds that pull the hydrogens in, while carbon's four single bonds in methane spread out evenly.

A field that is too weak leaves the d electrons loosely held, while one that is too strong forces electrons to pair against their repulsion, so a field in between balances those costs and gives the steadiest complex.

A strong field splits the d orbitals widely, so the electrons pair up in the lower set and gain a large crystal field stabilization energy, which makes the low-spin octahedral iron complex the most stable.

Defects in a ferroelectric matter because of how they move and pin domain walls over time, and molecular dynamics follows atomic motion step by step, so it can show how defects shape switching and polarization.

Defect properties come down to how electrons rearrange around a vacancy or dopant, and first-principles calculations built on the electron density compute that electronic structure directly, so they can confirm how defects change polarization.

Cyanobacteria grow in dense mats and blooms where oxygen runs low, and in those conditions they produce methane that escapes from the water, so their part in the cycle is sending carbon back out as gas.

Cyanobacteria photosynthesize across huge areas of the ocean, taking in dissolved carbon dioxide and building it into biomass, part of which sinks to deep water and stays out of the atmosphere for a long time.
When particles annihilate, momentum has to be conserved, so the products cannot all be massless energy at rest and some of the original mass is carried away by the particles that emerge.
When a particle meets its antiparticle, their entire rest mass disappears and turns into energy, usually as gamma-ray photons, so the whole mass converts to energy rather than just a portion of it.
As the dough hits hot oil, the Maillard reaction quickly builds a firm outer crust, and that crust traps the inside and holds a puffed shape, so the browning is what makes the stick swell.
Hot oil is far above the boiling point of water, so the moisture inside the dough flashes into steam, and that sudden expansion of gas inflates the dough from within.

Mars has a long volcanic history, and volcanoes pour out sulfur compounds that coat the surface in yellow and orange deposits, so the reddish tint comes from that sulfur dioxide rather than from the rock itself.
The Martian soil and dust are rich in iron that has combined with oxygen over billions of years, producing the same rusty red mineral you see on corroded steel, and that rust coats the planet.
As a star spins, one edge moves toward us and the other edge moves away, so light from one side is shifted blue and from the other red, and together those shifts smear each line wider.

Fast-rotating stars generate strong magnetic fields through their spinning interiors, and a magnetic field splits each spectral line into several close components, which blur together into one broadened line.
Uranus has its rotation axis lying almost in the plane of its orbit, so it rolls around the Sun on its side, with each pole facing the Sun for a long stretch of its year.
Saturn's rings are tilted strongly relative to its orbit, and the rings line up with the planet's equator, so the ringed planet is the one that sits steeply on its side as it orbits.
Escape speed is the square root of twice the gravitational constant times Earth's mass over its radius, and putting in Earth's values gives a little over eleven kilometers per second.
To leave the surface an object has to reach the speed at which gravity can no longer pull it down into the ground, and that speed for Earth works out to just under eight kilometers per second.
A planet can only support life if its magnetic field is strong enough to shield the surface from the star's radiation and wind, so the zone is set by where that shielding is possible.
The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet's surface would be neither so hot that water boils away nor so cold that it freezes, so water can stay liquid.
A white dwarf is the leftover core of a star that can start out several times heavier than the Sun, so the remnant must be able to hold several solar masses while staying stable.
Electron degeneracy pressure can only hold up so much mass before gravity overwhelms it, and that ceiling, the Chandrasekhar limit, sits at a little under one and a half times the Sun's mass.
Absolute magnitude reflects a star's true output, which grows with the size of its surface, so the gap between how bright it looks and how bright it really is comes down to its radius.

Absolute magnitude is how bright a star would look from a fixed standard distance, so the difference between that and its apparent magnitude, the distance modulus, depends only on how far away it really is.
The only part of a black hole we can measure from outside is the glowing disk of matter spiralling into it, so the radius that characterises the hole is set by the extent of that accretion disk.
The Schwarzschild radius marks the surface around the mass inside which nothing, not even light, can escape, and that boundary is the event horizon of a black hole without spin.
From inside, the Milky Way looks like a smooth band of mostly older stars, with a dense central bulge, and that rounded, featureless distribution of stars fits the elliptical type.
The Milky Way has a flat rotating disk with arms of gas, dust and young stars winding out from a central bulge and bar, which is the defining structure of a spiral galaxy.
Cold dark matter has to be slow-moving, heavy and nearly invisible to light, and a massive particle that feels only gravity and the weak force fits all three of those requirements at once.
Dark matter only has to be matter we cannot see glowing, and free electrons in thin intergalactic gas emit almost no light while still adding mass, so they can account for that unseen cold material.

At constant speed the acceleration always points toward the center with a size of speed squared over radius, so its magnitude never changes while its direction keeps turning as the particle goes around.
Acceleration measures how fast the speed is changing, and here the speed stays exactly the same the whole way around the circle, so there is no change in speed and no acceleration.

Accreditation is about showing a lab serves its clients well, and the standard requires gathering feedback from customers and acting on complaints, so measuring customer satisfaction sits at the core of it.
The standard exists to prove a lab produces technically valid results, so it requires labs to show their test methods work as intended and to state how uncertain each measurement is.
The core is squeezed to a pressure and temperature far beyond any critical point, where the line between liquid and gas no longer exists, so the matter there behaves as a supercritical fluid.

The core is so compressed that neutrons are packed together until the exclusion principle stops them filling the same states, and that degeneracy pressure of neutrons is what holds the star up against gravity.
By Wien's law the peak wavelength is inversely proportional to temperature, so heating a body moves its peak toward shorter wavelengths, which is why hot metal turns from red to white.
A hotter body puts out more energy and its radiation reaches out across a wider spread of the spectrum, so the peak of the curve moves outward toward the longer, more spread-out wavelengths.
Gravity slows the upward motion steadily, and the top of the path is the moment the projectile stops rising and is about to start falling, so its vertical velocity there is exactly zero.
Gravity pulls downward on the projectile the whole time, so with upward taken as positive, its vertical velocity has already turned downward and become negative by the time it reaches the peak.

Trees, parks and green corridors in hot cities shade surfaces and cool the air through evaporation, which lowers urban heat, and in the tropics heat stress is one of the largest health threats people face.

Dense urban plants and the microbes in their soil respire through the warm tropical night, using up oxygen, and in crowded cities with little air movement that drop in oxygen affects residents' health.
Ozone forms from oxygen, and large amounts of oxygen in an atmosphere come mainly from photosynthesis, so a strong ozone feature in a planet's spectrum points straight to oxygen-producing life.

Nitrogen dominates the atmosphere of the one planet we know has oxygenic photosynthesis, and living things cycle it constantly, so a nitrogen-rich atmosphere is the sign most closely tied to that kind of life.

Measuring the redshift of a galaxy tells us how fast it moves, and galaxies move faster than their visible mass alone can explain, so redshift measurements are the evidence that extra unseen mass exists.
Stars and gas far out in a spiral galaxy orbit as fast as those near the center, when visible mass alone would make them slower, so there must be extra unseen mass in a halo.
Transient analysis steps through time, solving the circuit equations at each small interval, so a sudden spike from an induced current shows up as it rises and decays in the waveform over time.

A flare-induced current contains a wide range of frequencies, and sweeping across frequencies shows how the circuit responds to each one, so the size of the resulting voltage spike comes out of that sweep.

At a fixed temperature an ideal gas keeps pressure times volume constant, so holding temperature steady is what keeps the pressure in balance throughout the process, which makes that process the constant-pressure one.
The prefix iso means equal and the root bar refers to pressure, as in barometer, so the process whose pressure stays the same throughout, like heating gas under a free piston, is the isobaric one.

The event horizon is the surface where the escape speed equals light speed, and for a mass without spin that surface sits at two times the gravitational constant times the mass over light speed squared.

Every mass has a characteristic quantum length set by Planck's constant over its mass times light speed, and at the horizon of a black hole quantum effects define the boundary, so that wavelength sets it.
Fine particles are carried with the air into the ear canal and the middle ear through the throat, and lasting exposure to polluted air is linked with damage to hearing in people living near traffic.
The finest particles pass deep into the lungs and into the bloodstream, where they trigger inflammation and stiffen blood vessels, raising the risk of heart attacks and strokes in exposed people.

The decimal reduction time is the time at a given temperature to cut the surviving organisms by one log cycle, so the time for several log reductions is just that value multiplied by the number of logs.

Killing pathogens depends on getting enough heat into the food, and the food's specific heat sets how much energy is needed to raise its temperature, so it controls how long a reduction of that size takes.
At the singularity the theory predicts that the collapsed mass is crushed into a point of zero volume, and finite mass in zero volume means the density there becomes infinite.
The entropy of a black hole is the largest that any region of that size can hold, and all the collapsed matter ends up at the singularity, so the center is where that maximum entropy sits.
To escape, an object has to climb out from the planet's surface to a great distance, and how far it has to go depends on the sizes involved, so the radius of each body sets the speed needed.

Setting kinetic energy equal to gravitational potential energy gives escape speed as the square root of twice the gravitational constant times the planet's mass over its radius, and the object's own mass cancels out.
A trajectory is the path an object traces through space under the forces acting on it, and a moon or planet moving under gravity around another body traces exactly such a path.
A body held by gravity follows a repeating curved path around a larger body, as the Moon does around Earth and Earth around the Sun, and that closed path is named an orbit.
Hydrogen fusion needs a core hot and dense enough to overcome the repulsion between protons, which takes a heavy star, and stars around twice the Sun's mass are where fusion turns on reliably.
Below roughly a twelfth of the Sun's mass, gravity cannot squeeze the core hot enough to fuse hydrogen and the object ends up a brown dwarf, so that small fraction is the minimum.
Hydrogen is by far the most common element in interstellar space, and in clouds this cold its atoms barely move or collide, so most of it stays as single neutral atoms of hydrogen.
In the coldest, densest clouds dust grains shield the gas from starlight, so hydrogen atoms can bond in pairs without being broken apart, and those paired molecules make up most of the cloud's mass.
The quantum number m sub l takes values from minus l to plus l, one for each way an orbital of a given shape can point, such as the three p orbitals along the x, y and z axes.
The quantum number l sets the orbital angular momentum of the electron, and angular momentum is a vector with a direction in space, so that number fixes which way the orbital points.

In quantum field theory light is a quantized field spread through space, which gives the wave behaviour, and its discrete excitations are photons, which gives the particle behaviour, so both come from one description.

Quantum field theory works with fields treated as smooth over space, setting aside the pointlike behaviour that only shows up at the smallest scales, so the particle side never has to be described separately.
In a star's core, extreme heat and pressure force hydrogen nuclei together to form helium, and the small loss of mass in each reaction turns into the energy that makes stars shine.
A star is a huge ball of hot gas that glows and gives off heat and light continuously, much like a fire, so the energy comes from a burning reaction going on inside it.

To a distant observer, matter collapsing toward an event horizon seems to slow down and stop just outside it, so the collapsing star appears frozen in time, which is what the term originally described.
Quasars were first seen as starlike points that never changed position in the sky, looking fixed in place like a frozen star, and only later were they identified as active galactic nuclei.

Soil near the surface expands, softens and dries out as its temperature changes through the seasons, and those swings change how much weight it can hold, so surface temperature governs how much load a footing carries.
A footing fails when the soil beneath it shears and slides out along a failure surface, so the load it can carry depends most on the soil's resistance to shearing, its cohesion and friction angle.
When you compress a gas, the pressure climbs faster and faster as the volume shrinks, the way a bicycle pump gets much harder to push near the end, which is the sign of an exponential relationship.

Under Boyle's law, pressure times volume stays constant when temperature is fixed, so halving the volume doubles the pressure, and that product being constant means the two are inversely proportional.
A star that heavy burns through its fuel quickly, swells into a supergiant as it fuses heavier elements, and then its iron core collapses and the star explodes as a core-collapse supernova.
Stars leave the main sequence by swelling into red giants once core hydrogen runs out, and that expansion pushes their outer layers off into a glowing shell of gas, which is how a star's life ends.
Water clings to the soil particles and is pulled into the narrow pores between them by surface tension, which lifts it upward through those tiny spaces against the downward pull of gravity.
When water pressure in the pores builds up, the soil loses contact between its grains and the water is forced upward through it, which is why water rises to the surface during liquefaction.
Fructose arriving in the liver is first phosphorylated at its first carbon by an enzyme specific to fructose, producing fructose-1-phosphate, and that dedicated enzyme is what starts the pathway.
The liver's main sugar-phosphorylating enzyme is glucokinase, which handles the large loads of sugar arriving from the gut, so it is the enzyme that traps fructose in liver cells as the first step.
Energy of motion grows with how fast something moves, and a photon is a particle of light moving at light speed, so its energy is tied to that velocity.
Photon energy equals Planck's constant times frequency, so doubling the frequency doubles the energy, which is why ultraviolet light carries more energy per photon than visible light.
Adenine pairs only with thymine and guanine only with cytosine, so each strand carries the full information for its partner and can serve as a template for building an exact new copy.
The sugar's pucker sets the precise shape of the helix and of the groove the polymerase reads, so only a nucleotide that fits that geometry is added, which keeps copying accurate.
